notes:
Task and constraints: Find which receptor is reached by a ray bouncing between square-room walls.
Idea: Compute the least common multiple of room width p and vertical step q, then inspect parity of the reflection counts.
Technique and why it applies: The unfolded ray reaches a corner after L/q vertical traversals and L/p horizontal traversals; parity identifies the receptor.
Invariant: L is the shared travel scale where both coordinates align with a wall corner.
Edge cases: lcm is used without import in the snippet. p and q are assumed positive and q no greater than p.
Complexity: With a built-in LCM, time and space are O(1); otherwise Euclid's algorithm is logarithmic.

Task and constraints: Identify the receptor reached by the reflected ray.
Idea: Compute lcm(p,q) using a local Euclidean gcd, then classify the parity of horizontal and vertical traversal counts.
Technique and why it applies: Odd/even parity of lcm divided by each room dimension determines which corner the ray reaches.
Invariant: gcd reduces the dimensions and lcm gives the first shared corner alignment.
Edge cases: Positive p and q are assumed. The three parity cases return receptors 0, 1, or 2.
Complexity: Euclid's algorithm takes O(log min(p,q)) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine the receptor reached by a ray reflecting inside a square room.
Idea: Compare the lowest set-bit values of p and q to infer their powers-of-two parity relationship.
Technique and why it applies: The bit trick p & -p extracts the least significant set bit; relative values determine which dimensions have an odd quotient at the first corner alignment.
Invariant: The comparison encodes the same parity cases as the LCM solution.
Edge cases: p and q are positive integers; zero would make the bitwise interpretation invalid for the geometric problem.
Complexity: The method uses O(1) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether two strings can become equal by swapping exactly two characters in the first string.
Idea: Collect mismatched characters and compare them crosswise; when strings already match, require a duplicate character.
Technique and why it applies: Exactly two mismatches must reverse each other, while an unchanged string needs two equal characters to swap without changing the result.
Invariant: diffCharactersInS and diffCharactersInGoal store mismatches in corresponding order.
Edge cases: Length mismatch fails immediately. Counter is used only for the equal-string duplicate case.
Complexity: The scan and optional count take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether one swap can make A equal B.
Idea: Collect at most two mismatched character pairs and check whether they are reverses.
Technique and why it applies: Two mismatches must cross-match; zero mismatches succeeds only if A contains a duplicate character that can be swapped harmlessly.
Invariant: diff stores mismatched character pairs in position order.
Edge cases: The early return rejects more than two mismatches. itertools is imported but unused.
Complexity: The scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for at most two mismatch pairs.

Task and constraints: Decide whether correct change can be returned for each lemonade customer.
Idea: Track counts of five- and ten-dollar bills and greedily give change for ten and twenty.
Technique and why it applies: A ten-dollar bill requires one five; a twenty is paid with one ten plus five when possible, otherwise three fives.
Invariant: five and ten record the available change inventory after each customer.
Edge cases: The branch ordering correctly prefers using a ten and a five for a twenty. Any unsupported bill value falls into the failure path.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether every lemonade customer can receive exact change.
Idea: Maintain five- and ten-dollar counts, preferring one ten plus one five for a twenty-dollar bill.
Technique and why it applies: A ten-dollar payment consumes a five; a twenty consumes either ten-and-five or three fives.
Invariant: five and ten represent the current cash inventory.
Edge cases: The final else treats every bill other than 5 or 10 as a 20, relying on the problem's allowed denominations.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether all customers can receive change using the greedy coin inventory.
Idea: Add each incoming bill to counts, then greedily use available 10- and 5-dollar coins to make the required change.
Technique and why it applies: The change amount is bill minus five; available denominations are tried from largest to smallest.
Invariant: counts tracks bill denominations, and change tracks the unpaid remainder.
Edge cases: The implementation counts the incoming bill before making change, which could allow using the customer's own bill as change; with denominations, change needs only smaller coins, so that larger bill is not selected.
Complexity: The loop is O(n) time and O(1) denomination space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the binary score of a matrix by flipping rows and columns.
Idea: Treat each row's first bit as the desired leading one and compute each column's best count after row normalization.
Technique and why it applies: XOR with the first column models the row flip; each column then contributes its larger one/zero count times its binary place value.
Invariant: col counts effective ones in the current column after row flips.
Edge cases: The matrix is assumed nonempty and rectangular; the first column becomes all ones after normalization.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest nonempty subarray with sum at least K, allowing negative values.
Idea: Build prefix sums and maintain an increasing deque of candidate prefix indices.
Technique and why it applies: A qualifying prefix difference yields a valid subarray; popping from the front records the shortest candidate, while dominated larger prefixes are removed from the back.
Invariant: monoq stores indices with strictly increasing prefix sums.
Edge cases: deque is referenced without import. Negative numbers invalidate ordinary sliding-window assumptions, which this monotonic deque handles.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and space O(n), since each prefix index is added and removed at most once.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest subarray whose sum is at least K.
Idea: Build prefix sums and use a monotonic deque to maintain candidate start indices.
Technique and why it applies: When the current prefix is large enough above the front prefix, record the length and remove that start; remove dominated prefixes from the back.
Invariant: mono_increasing_q holds indices with increasing accumulated sums.
Edge cases: Negative values are supported. If no qualifying subarray exists, the method returns -1.
Complexity: Each prefix index enters and leaves the deque at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum moves needed to collect every key in a grid with locks and walls.
Idea: Use BFS over position and collected-key string, expanding valid neighboring cells one step at a time.
Technique and why it applies: A lock is traversable only if its matching lowercase key is present; BFS layer count gives the shortest distance.
Invariant: visited stores position-and-key states, and q stores states awaiting exploration.
Edge cases: deque is used without an import. keyCt counts lowercase cells rather than distinct key letters, so repeated keys could make the completion test inaccurate; standard inputs have unique keys.
Complexity: The state space is O(RC·2^K) in the intended bitmask formulation, though string states can add overhead.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest path collecting all keys in a grid.
Idea: Precompute shortest distances between special locations, then run Dijkstra over location and collected-key bitmask.
Technique and why it applies: BFS distances between keys/locks are combined in a weighted state graph; a lock transition is allowed only when its key bit is set.
Invariant: best[place][state] stores the shortest distance for a location and key mask.
Edge cases: The distance BFS treats special locations as stopping points. The target mask assumes keys use distinct lowercase letters and all are represented in locations.
Complexity: With L special locations and K keys, state search is roughly O(L·2^K log(L·2^K)) after grid BFS preprocessing.

Task and constraints: Find the smallest prime palindrome greater than or equal to N.
Idea: Generate odd-length palindromes by mirroring the first half and test each candidate for primality.
Technique and why it applies: All even-length palindromes except 11 are divisible by 11, so the special case handles that length before generating odd-length candidates.
Invariant: i supplies the left half and j is the mirrored palindrome candidate.
Edge cases: If no candidate is found before i reaches 10^5, the function falls through without a return. The usual problem bound is intended to make a candidate appear.
Complexity: Each primality test costs O(sqrt(j)); the candidate search is bounded by the chosen half range.

Task and constraints: Transpose a rectangular matrix.
Idea: Allocate a result with reversed dimensions and assign each original cell to the swapped row and column.
Technique and why it applies: The coordinate mapping A[r][c] becomes result[c][r], which exchanges rows and columns.
Invariant: result stores the transposed matrix without changing A.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty matrix because it reads A[0]. Values are copied unchanged.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(RC) time and O(RC) output space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum distance between consecutive ones in the binary representation.
Idea: Scan the binary string after its leading prefix and update the gap whenever another one appears.
Technique and why it applies: The index difference between consecutive set bits gives their separation; the maximum such difference is the binary gap.
Invariant: prev stores the prior one position in the sliced bit string and res stores the best gap.
Edge cases: The slice bin(n)[3:] skips the initial binary prefix and first significant bit; for n with only one set bit, the answer remains zero.
Complexity: The scan takes O(log n) time and O(log n) string space.

Task and constraints: Compute the largest gap between consecutive set bits.
Idea: Inspect each of the lowest 32 bits and track positions where the bit is one.
Technique and why it applies: The difference between current and previous set-bit positions is the number of binary positions between their indices.
Invariant: last stores the previous set-bit index and result stores the largest gap.
Edge cases: The loop assumes relevant values fit in 32 bits; for larger integers, higher set bits are ignored.
Complexity: The method takes O(1) time under a fixed 32-bit bound and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Reorder nums1 to maximize positions where its value exceeds nums2 at the same index.
Idea: Sort nums1 and use a max-heap to process nums2 from largest value downward.
Technique and why it applies: If the largest remaining nums1 value beats the current largest nums2 value, use it; otherwise sacrifice the smallest value at that position.
Invariant: l and r delimit unused nums1 values, while the heap prioritizes largest nums2 values.
Edge cases: heapq is referenced without an import. Each nums1 value is assigned exactly once to the selected index.
Complexity: Sorting and heap operations take O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Construct an advantage shuffle maximizing wins against B.
Idea: Sort both arrays and assign each A value that beats the smallest remaining sorted B value; otherwise reserve it as a sacrifice.
Technique and why it applies: Greedily pairing a winning value to the smallest beatable opponent preserves larger values for harder opponents.
Invariant: candidates maps B values to assigned winning A values, and others stores values unable to beat the current opponent.
Edge cases: The dictionary uses B values as keys, so duplicate B values share one bucket and can make the assignment logic incorrect for duplicates.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n); assignment and output take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum refueling stops needed to reach target with initial fuel F.
Idea: Process stations in position order, storing available fuel amounts in a max-heap and refueling when the next position is unreachable.
Technique and why it applies: When fuel is insufficient, the largest previously passed fuel supply minimizes the number of stops needed.
Invariant: heap stores negative station fuels so the largest amount is popped first; ans counts stops.
Edge cases: The method appends a synthetic target station to S, mutating the input. heapq is not imported, so it requires an external import.
Complexity: Sorting is not performed; the stations must already be position-sorted. Heap operations give O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
